blocks.text: 1. Precision At K

blocks.alt: Top-K chunks produce relevant chunks, giving a precision score

blocks.text: Hybrid Retrieval closed the Graph RAG module by combining graph traversal with vector search. Precision at K, the fraction of the top K retrieved chunks that are actually relevant, opens this dedicated Evaluation module by naming the first concrete way to measure retrieval quality with a real number.
It counts how many of the top K results actually matter and divides by K.
2. Why Measuring Retrieval Quality Matters
As covered generally in Advanced RAG as measuring whether added steps help, every retrieval technique covered throughout this course needs an actual number to compare against.
Precision at K is the first, most direct such number this module covers.
3. Defining Relevant For This Metric
As with top-k selection in Re-Ranking, a retrieved chunk counts as relevant only if it actually helps answer the specific query.
A chunk about the right general topic but the wrong specific fact still counts as not relevant.

blocks.text: 4. The K In Precision At K Is A Choice

blocks.alt: Precision at 3 is compared against precision at 10

blocks.text: Choosing K equal to five versus K equal to ten produces different precision scores for the same retrieval.
K should match how many chunks the pipeline actually uses downstream.
5. Precision Ignores Rank Order Within K

blocks.alt: Relevant first is compared against relevant last, giving the same precision

blocks.text: As with top-k selection in Re-Ranking, a relevant chunk ranked first counts exactly the same as one ranked last within the top K.
Precision at K treats every position inside the cutoff equally.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Two retrievals with the same three relevant chunks out of five score identically on precision at K even if one puts the most useful chunk first and the other puts it last.

blocks.text: 6. Precision Says Something Different Than Recall

blocks.alt: Precision measures of retrieved how many relevant, while recall measures of relevant how many retrieved

blocks.text: Precision at K measures how much of what was retrieved is actually useful.
It says nothing about whether every relevant chunk in the whole knowledge base was actually found.
7. A High Precision Can Still Mean A Missed Answer

blocks.alt: High precision is compared against missing the actual answer

blocks.text: As with multi-hop questions benefiting most in Chain Of Thought, all five retrieved chunks being relevant does not guarantee the one chunk containing the actual answer was retrieved.
A perfect precision score can still coexist with a wrong final answer.

blocks.text: 8. Averaging Precision Across Many Queries

blocks.alt: Query 1 precision and query 2 precision average into overall precision

blocks.text: A single query's precision score says little about the system as a whole.
Averaging precision at K across a real evaluation set gives a trustworthy system level number.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A single query scoring perfect precision could be a lucky outlier; averaging precision at K across dozens or hundreds of representative queries is what actually characterizes the system.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Precision At K Is The Right Metric To Track

blocks.alt: Caring about top result quality points toward tracking precision at K

blocks.text: A system where irrelevant retrieved chunks actively hurt the final answer benefits from tracking precision.
A system where missing a fact matters more than noise, by contrast, should track recall instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates computing precision at K for a single query and averaging it across several queries.

code.content:
def precision_at_k(retrieved_chunks, relevant_chunk_ids, k):
    # only look at the top K retrieved chunks
    top_k = retrieved_chunks[:k]
    relevant_count = sum(1 for chunk_id in top_k if chunk_id in relevant_chunk_ids)
    return relevant_count / k

queries = [
    {"retrieved": ["c1", "c2", "c3", "c4", "c5"], "relevant": {"c1", "c3", "c4"}},
    {"retrieved": ["c6", "c7", "c8", "c9", "c10"], "relevant": {"c6", "c8"}},
]

k = 5
scores = [precision_at_k(q["retrieved"], q["relevant"], k) for q in queries]

print("Precision at K per query:")
for i, score in enumerate(scores):
    print(f"  Query {i + 1}: {score:.2f}")

# average across the evaluation set
average_precision = sum(scores) / len(scores)
print(f"\nAverage precision at K across the evaluation set: {average_precision:.2f}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows each query scoring a different precision based purely on how many of its top five retrieved chunks were actually relevant, then averaged into one system level number.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using a K value that does not match how many chunks the pipeline actually consumes downstream.
Treating precision at K as a complete quality measure when it says nothing about coverage.
Judging system quality from a single query's precision score instead of averaging over many.
Counting a chunk as relevant just because it mentions the right general topic.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Precision at K is the fraction of the top K retrieved chunks that are actually relevant.
A chunk counts as relevant only if it actually helps answer the specific query.
K should match how many chunks the pipeline actually uses downstream.
Precision at K treats every position within the top K equally, ignoring rank order.
Precision measures usefulness of what was retrieved, not whether everything relevant was found.
A perfect precision score can still coexist with a wrong final answer if the answer was missed.
Averaging precision at K across a real evaluation set gives a trustworthy system level number.
Next up: Recall at K, covering whether every relevant chunk was actually found.
